1.e4 e6 2.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre with two pawns and invites Black to challenge them, usually with ...d5, which attacks the e4-pawn at once. White gains space and a firm grip on the centre, but the d4-pawn becomes Black's usual target and the fate of the e-pawn has to be settled early. Whether the game turns closed or open depends on how White answers.
1.e4 e6 2.d4.name: French Defence: Normal Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d3.name: French Defence: King's Indian Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d3.background: The King's Indian Attack most often arises against the French Defence, usually after 2...d5 3.Nd2. Leading players such as Benko, Fischer, Stein and Psakhis have used 2.d3, and Fischer won with it against Myagmarsuren at the Sousse Interzonal of 1967.
1.e4 e6 2.d3.strategy: Prepares a flexible set-up with a fianchettoed king's bishop, early castling and the e4-e5 advance in reserve. White gives up the fight for the centre at once and gets a solid, closed position with no d4-pawn for Black to attack, aiming for space and play against the kingside. Black has time to build up on the queenside.

1.e4 e6 2.Nc3.name: French Defence: Queen's Knight
1.e4 e6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and defends e4, keeping the usual French set-ups available. Black can also leave the French structure and challenge White's centre from the side with the c-pawn, which leads to a slower, closed game. Sound, but it offers nothing that 2.d4 does not.

1.e4 e6 2.Nf3.name: French Defence: Knight Variation
1.e4 e6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and keeps d4 in reserve, so the game can still reach the usual French structures. Black can also leave them and challenge the centre with the c-pawn. Playable, but White has no reason to prefer it to 2.d4.

1.e4 e6 2.Qe2.name: French Defence: Chigorin Variation
1.e4 e6 2.Qe2.strategy: Puts the queen on the e-file, so that after 2...d5 3.exd5 the e6-pawn is pinned and Black has to recapture with the queen. Black therefore usually challenges the centre with the c-pawn first. The queen blocks the f1-bishop's diagonal, which is why White fianchettoes it.

1.e4 e6 2.c4.name: French Defence: Steiner Variation
1.e4 e6 2.c4.strategy: Takes aim at d5 to discourage 2...d5, but Black can still play it: after 3.cxd5 exd5 4.exd5 Nf6, White keeps the extra pawn only with 5.Bb5+, and Black gets good compensation for it.

1.e4 e6 2.b3.name: French Defence: Horwitz Attack
1.e4 e6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 to put pressure on the long diagonal and on g7. After 2...d5 3.Bb2 dxe4 White has given the e-pawn for quick development. Rare, risky and not recommended, though not refuted.

1.e4 e6 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 with pawn support, but takes c3 from the queen's knight: after ...d5 and ...dxe4 it can recapture only from d2. Black can also challenge the centre with the c-pawn at once. Sound, but no improvement on 2.d4.

1.e4 e6 2.e5.name: French Defence: Steinitz Attack
1.e4 e6 2.e5.strategy: Advances the pawn before the centre is ready. 2...d6 hits it at once and gives White no advantage, since exd6 Bxd6 only helps Black's development; and if Black plays 2...d5 and White 3.d4, the position is one White could have reached with 2.d4 d5 3.e5, so the early advance gains nothing.

1.e4 e6 2.Bb5.name: French Defence: Bird Invitation
1.e4 e6 2.Bb5.background: Introduced by Henry Bird during the Vienna 1873 tournament and little played since.
1.e4 e6 2.Bb5.strategy: Pins the d7-pawn against the king so that 2...d5 is not possible at once. But 2...c6 or 2...a6 attacks the bishop, and once it retreats Black plays ...d5 with a gain of time.

1.e4 e6 2.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop onto a diagonal that the e6-pawn already blocks, and 2...d5 hits it at once: after 3.exd5 exd5 it has to move again, to b3 or d3, and White has lost a tempo while Black has the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.f4.name: French Defence: La Bourdonnais Variation
1.e4 e6 2.f4.background: Named after Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais, a 19th-century French master.
1.e4 e6 2.f4.strategy: Supports a later e5 and claims space, but develops nothing and weakens the e1-h4 diagonal and the squares e3 and g3. Black takes the centre at once and can challenge an advanced e-pawn with the c-pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.g3.name: French Defence: Réti-Spielmann Attack
1.e4 e6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 but is slow against 2...d5: 3.d3 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ costs White the right to castle, and 3.Bg2 dxe4 4.Bxe4 Nf6 gains Black a tempo on the bishop.

1.e4 e6 2.b4.name: French Defence: Banzai-Leong Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.b4.strategy: Gives up the b-pawn to gain time: after 2...Bxb4 3.c3 the bishop has to move again and White can build a pawn centre, but the centre does not make up for the pawn, and Black develops freely.

1.e4 e6 2.Be2.strategy: Prepares castling but does nothing for the centre and takes e2 from the g1-knight. After 2...d5 White still has to settle the attack on e4, while Black develops freely.

1.e4 e6 2.Bd3.strategy: Blocks the d-pawn, so the central break d4 is unavailable until the bishop moves again, and 2...d5 challenges e4 at once.

1.e4 e6 2.Ne2.strategy: Develops the knight, but it blocks the f1-bishop and the queen's diagonal and does not contest the centre. After 2...d5 Black has the easier game.

1.e4 e6 2.Na3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, heading for c4 or b5 but doing nothing for the centre. Black can take the centre at once or double White's a-pawns with 2...Bxa3 3.bxa3.

1.e4 e6 2.Nh3.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, heading for f4, but does nothing for the centre. Black takes the centre at once, and once the e6-pawn leaves the c8-h3 diagonal, ...Bxh3 gxh3 can wreck White's kingside pawns.

1.e4 e6 2.Qf3.strategy: Takes f3 from the king's knight and aims at f7, but an early queen achieves little: Black develops with tempo, takes the centre, and f7 is easy to defend.

1.e4 e6 2.Qg4.strategy: Eyes g7, but the Bf8 guards it, so there is no threat. 2...Nf6 hits the queen and e4 at once and Black develops with tempo.

1.e4 e6 2.Qh5.strategy: Aims at f7, but the e6-pawn already shuts out a bishop on c4, so f7 is safe; 2...Nf6 gains a tempo by attacking the queen.

1.e4 e6 2.f3.strategy: Supports e4 but takes f3 from the g1-knight and opens the e1-h4 diagonal, so that 2...Qh4+ forces 3.g3 or a king move. Black can also simply take the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.g4.strategy: Gains kingside space but does nothing for the centre or development and loosens the pawns in front of the king. Black takes the centre at once and can attack the g4-pawn with ...h5.

1.e4 e6 2.h4.strategy: A flank pawn move that develops nothing, does nothing for the centre and loosens the kingside. Black replies 2...d5 and White has lost a tempo.

1.e4 e6 2.h3.strategy: A waiting move that stops ...Bg4 but does nothing for the centre or development. Black challenges e4 at once, with White's pieces still at home.

1.e4 e6 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4 and a queenside expansion, but loses a tempo; 2...d5 takes the centre and White has nothing to show for the time spent.

1.e4 e6 2.a4.strategy: A wing pawn move that neither develops a piece nor fights for the centre; ...d5 challenges e4, and White has developed nothing.

1.e4 e6 2.Ke2.strategy: Forfeits castling and shuts in the f1-bishop and the queen for nothing. Black takes the centre with 2...d5, and the king stands on the e-file, which opens as soon as pawns are exchanged on d5.

1.e4 e6 2.Ba6.strategy: Loses a piece for nothing: the bishop attacks only b7, which the Bc8 guards, and 2...bxa6 or 2...Nxa6 simply takes it.

1.e4 e6.name: French Defence
1.e4 e6.background: Named after a correspondence match between London and Paris in 1834, in which the Paris side, persuaded by Jacques Chamouillet, adopted it. Wilhelm Steinitz called it “the dullest of all openings”, yet for several decades it has been the third most popular reply to 1.e4, after 1...c5 and 1...e5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once and claims a share of the centre. The cost is the pawn chain on e6 and d5, which shuts in the light-squared bishop on c8, and Black usually looks for counterplay by hitting White's centre at its base with ...c5. White chooses how to hold or release the tension, so the game can become closed or open.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Bb4+.strategy: Checks at once and, if White blocks with the knight, Black pins it and challenges the centre with ...d5. But blocking with a pawn simply forces the bishop back, and blocking with the bishop offers a trade of Black's dark-squared bishop, so Black has gained little for the time spent.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6.strategy: Keeps a White bishop off b5 and prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7 against e4, while Black can still build a French-style centre. The cost is a tempo on a rim pawn move, and White can answer by taking space and developing freely. It leads to an unorthodox game in which Black hopes to attack the centre from the wing.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop against e4 and a flexible set-up for the knights. White can support the centre and keep more space.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5.name: French Defence: Franco-Sicilian Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and aims to trade the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, with ...e6 already played. White can give extra space or open the game. A rare sideline, not refuted but less sound than challenging the centre at once with the d-pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d6.name: Rat Defence: Small Centre Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d6.strategy: Keeps the centre compact with pawns on e6 and d6 and aims for quick development and castling, with a pawn break in the centre later. Without ...d5 Black stays passive and White can take more space or develop freely.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops and presses on d4, but blocks the c7-pawn, so the usual French break ...c5 against d4 is no longer at hand. White keeps more space and can even drive the knight back with d5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Na6.strategy: Heads for b4 or c7, but on a6 the knight stands offside and does nothing against the centre. White can take b4 away with 3.a3 and keeps the larger centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Qe7.strategy: Puts the queen in front of the f8 bishop and takes e7 from the knight, yet does nothing to challenge the centre. White develops freely and keeps the space advantage.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early against d4 and takes f6 from the knight. White develops with gain of time, for instance 3.Nc3 with Nd5 or e5 to follow against the queen.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Qh4.strategy: Attacks the e4-pawn, but White defends it with a developing move, and gains more time later by attacking the queen with a knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop modestly before ...d5 and leaves g7 without its defender, so 3.Qg4 attacks it at once. Otherwise White keeps the larger centre with simple development, as the bishop on e7 does not bear on d4.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Bd6.strategy: Blocks the d7-pawn, so ...d5 is impossible for now, and puts the bishop on a square that 3.e5 attacks at once. Taking on e5 gives the bishop for a pawn after dxe5, so it retreats, and White has gained space and time.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where e4 and the queen cover its forward squares f5 and g4, so it does nothing against the centre. White develops freely and keeps the larger centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Nf6.name: French Defence: Mediterranean Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 but allows 3.e5, which drives the knight away: after 3...Nd5 4.c4 it has to move a third time, and White has gained space and time before Black has played ...d5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the f8 bishop, which can come out only after ...g6 or once the knight moves on, and puts no pressure on d4 or e4. White develops freely and keeps the larger centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a wing move that neither develops a piece nor challenges the centre, and weakens b5. White uses the time to develop.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a pawn triangle on c6, d5 and e6 that shuts in the c8 bishop, which cannot come out to f5. White can then close the centre with e5 and gain space, and Black's ...c5 break costs a second tempo.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 f6.strategy: Takes e5 and prepares ...e5, but opens the e8-h5 diagonal: 3.Qh5+ forces ...g6 or ...Ke7, and the king loses its cover. The pawn also takes the best square from the knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5.name: French Defence: Franco-Hiva Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5.strategy: Attacks e4 in Dutch style, but after 3.exf5 exf5 the e-file and the e8-h5 diagonal lie open in front of Black's king, and the f5-pawn needs defending against Bd3. White develops quickly, and Black has no compensation for the loosened position.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 against d4, but with pawns on e6 and g6 the dark squares f6 and h6 are weak, and h4 followed by h5 can strike at g6. Otherwise White simply takes the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 h6.strategy: Prevents Bg5, which is no threat yet because the queen would simply take the bishop. It wastes a tempo that White uses to develop.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 h5.strategy: Weakens g5 and g6 for good and neither develops a piece nor challenges the centre. White uses the tempo to develop.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Qg5.strategy: Hangs the queen: the bishop's diagonal c1-g5 is open after d4, and 3.Bxg5 wins her for nothing.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the f8 bishop. 3.Bg5+ follows at once, and Black must block or move the king again, so it stays stuck in the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Bc5.strategy: Puts the bishop en prise to the d-pawn: 3.dxc5 wins it, and no Black piece can recapture.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.Nxa3 or 3.bxa3 takes it, and nothing recaptures, so Black is a whole piece down.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 b5.name: French Defence: Baeuerle Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn for play on the long diagonal with ...Bb7. After 3.Bxb5 Bb7 White can defend e4 and keep the extra pawn, as Black's activity hardly compensates.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 g5.strategy: Weakens the kingside for nothing: after 3.Nf3 the pawn is attacked by knight and bishop and defended only by the queen, so Black must defend or advance it and loses time and structure.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Pushes the e-pawn a second time straight into 3.dxe5, and no Black piece can recapture at once. Black has spent two moves on the e-pawn only to give it up.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once and claims the centre, the standard French answer. White keeps the pawn on e4 protected with pieces and aims for a slow, closed game, usually a kingside fianchetto with castling, and a later e4-e5 push that cramps Black and prepares a kingside attack. Black gets a solid centre and play on the queenside, at the price of being the one defending against that bind.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 c5.strategy: Controls d4 and keeps ...d5 in reserve. Black can still choose the central set-up or hold the d-pawn back for a while. The price is that e4 stays unchallenged for the moment, so White may also build a closed set-up, a quiet game of slow manoeuvring.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and controls d4 and e5, but blocks the c-pawn, so the usual French break ...c5 needs the knight to move again. Sound enough, yet less precise than a central pawn move, which keeps Black's options open.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4, which d3 already covers, and usually leads to the central pawn set-up anyway. Sound and flexible, but it also allows 3.e5, which gains space with tempo on the knight, while 2...d5 states the central claim first.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Be7.strategy: A solid developing move that prepares castling and keeps the central pawn breaks in reserve. It is slow, because it does nothing against e4, and White completes the set-up undisturbed.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against e4, for a flexible set-up. Sound, but slow: the d3-pawn keeps e4 firmly protected, and White develops at leisure.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn triangle on c6, d5 and e6. It is sound but passive: ...c5 later costs a second move with the c-pawn, and the b8-knight loses its natural square c6.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d6.strategy: A solid but passive set-up: the pawns on d6 and e6 cover e5 and d5 and open d7 for the c8-bishop, but a later ...d5 costs a second move with the d-pawn. White develops and castles undisturbed.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and ...Ne7, a fianchetto that keeps the central pawn breaks in reserve. Sound, but slow: e4 stays unchallenged, and the open c1–h6 diagonal lets White aim Qd2 and Bh6 at the bishop on g7.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Na6.strategy: A rim knight that eyes nothing in the centre and only hopes for ...Nc7 later. It neither contests e4 nor prepares ...d5, so White simply develops and builds the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Qe7.strategy: Blocks the f8-bishop and clutters the kingside, so development stalls. White gains time while the queen stands in its own pieces' way.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Qf6.strategy: An early queen sortie that takes f6 from the g8-knight and threatens nothing, since b2 and f2 are both covered. White simply develops with gain of time against the queen.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Qh4.strategy: The queen is driven back at once by Nf3 or g3, so White develops with tempo. The sortie wastes time and leaves the rest of Black's pieces undeveloped.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Bd6.strategy: Blocks the d7-pawn, so the French strike ...d5 is impossible until the bishop moves again, and the c8-bishop stays shut in. White develops freely.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Bc5.strategy: Puts the bishop where 3.d4 attacks it with tempo, so White gets the full centre while the bishop has to lose time retreating.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Bb4+.strategy: The check achieves nothing: 3.c3 drives the bishop back and prepares d4, and 3.Bd2 offers a trade that helps White's development. Either way Black loses time.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Nh6.strategy: A rim knight that allows Bxh6 gxh6, wrecking the kingside pawns, and in return does nothing for the centre or for ...d5.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Ne7.strategy: Shuts in the f8-bishop, whose only open diagonal runs through e7, so it needs another knight move or ...g6 to come out. White meanwhile develops freely.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 a6.strategy: A slow wing move that neither develops a piece nor prepares ...d5. White develops or plays d4 with a free hand.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 a5.strategy: Takes queenside space and stops b4, but spends a tempo without developing anything and leaves a permanent hole on b5. White uses the time to develop.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 b5.strategy: A premature queenside advance that weakens c6 and the long diagonal a8-h1 and does nothing for ...d5. A quick a4 undermines the pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal, so 3.Qh5+ forces ...g6 or ...Ke7 and loosens the king position further. Its only point is to support ...e5, a second move with the e-pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 f5.name: French Defence: King's Indian Attack, Franco-Hiva Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d3 f5.strategy: A gambit try that weakens the king's position. After 3.exf5, ...exf5 opens the e-file for Qe2+, while 3...Nf6 4.fxe6 leaves Black a pawn down without enough development in return.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 g5.strategy: Advances the g-pawn without developing anything, weakening f6, h6 and the dark squares around the king. White can undermine it with h4 and take the centre meanwhile.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 h6.strategy: A slow prophylactic move against Bg5 that does not develop a piece or fight for the centre; White uses the time to develop.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 h5.strategy: A slow flank move that weakens g5 and g6, helps neither development nor ...d5, and hands White a free developing move.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 e5.strategy: Gives up the French pawn structure after spending two moves with the e-pawn. Black reaches a King's Pawn Game with ...e5 a tempo down, and White builds freely.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Qg5.strategy: Walks into Bxg5, because the c1-bishop sees g5 along the open diagonal c1-d2-e3-f4. The queen is lost for nothing.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for no reason and blocks both the f8-bishop and the queen's d8–h4 diagonal. 3.Bg5+ then forces ...f6, ...Nf6 into a pin, or another king move.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 Ba3.strategy: Puts the bishop where 3.bxa3 or 3.Nxa3 takes it, so Black simply loses a piece.

1.e4 e6 2.b3 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once, as Black does against any French set-up; White's quiet queenside move has done nothing to stop it. The pawn immediately questions e4, which nothing defends yet, so White has to react and Black gets the easier game.

1.e4 e6 2.b4 Bxb4.strategy: Accepts the gambit: the pawn is free and the bishop develops by taking it, without being attacked or giving White an immediate target. White's only compensation is a hope of faster development, so Black needs only to develop sensibly and look after the bishop.

1.e4 e6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre anyway: White's c-pawn did not prevent the French pawn on d5, and it hits e4 at once. White must now decide how to resolve the tension, and Black keeps a sound game whichever way it goes.

1.e4 e6 2.f4 d5.strategy: The natural French reply: Black strikes at the e4 pawn at once, and f4 has done nothing to protect it. White's move aims at e5 and a kingside attack, but it opens the e1–h4 diagonal in front of the king, so Black is the one with a clear target.

1.e4 e6 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: The move that makes it a French: Black hits e4 at once. The knight defends it, so there is no gain yet, but Black has claimed a share of the centre before White has built the d4–e4 pair, and the game most likely becomes an ordinary French.

1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: The standard French reply: Black challenges e4, which the knight on f3 does not defend, so White has to settle the tension at once. Black reaches the usual French pawn structure with the choice of how to meet White's decision.

1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: The same idea as against 2.d4: a flank pawn lunges at e4 before a single piece is out. White can simply take it, and after the recapture on f5 the e-file and the e8–h5 diagonal are open in front of the king, with nothing gained in return.
1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 f5.name: French Defence: Knight Variation, Franco-Hiva Gambit

1.e4 e6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2.name: French Defence: Horwitz Attack, Papa-Ticulat Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2.strategy: Develops the bishop to the long diagonal, where it eyes g7, and leaves the e4 pawn to Black. White hopes for quick development and pressure along the diagonal in return; if Black takes the pawn, White has to show that the compensation is real, which makes this an offbeat way to play.

1.e4 e6 2.b4 Bxb4 3.e5.name: French Defence: Banzai-Leong Gambit, Pinova Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.b4 Bxb4 3.e5.strategy: Gains space and keeps the g8 knight from its natural square, since a knight on f6 would be captured. But Black is a pawn up, the bishop on b4 is not attacked, and the pawn on e5 itself has no defender, so White has given a pawn for little more than space.

1.e4 e6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5.strategy: Releases the tension by capturing, removing Black's central pawn and leaving White a half-open c-file to play against c7. If Black recaptures with the e-pawn, White can take again and win a pawn, though Black gets good compensation for it.

1.e4 e6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 exd5.strategy: Recaptures towards the centre, so that Black has a pawn on d5 attacking e4 again. The departure of the e-pawn also frees the c8-bishop, which was shut in behind e6. White can win a pawn with exd5, but Black gets good compensation for it.

1.e4 e6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 exd5 4.Qb3.name: French Defence: Orthoschnapp Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 exd5 4.Qb3.strategy: Brings the queen out early to hit d5 and b7, but nothing is really threatened: the bishop guards b7, and Black simply takes the e-pawn, ending a pawn up. White hopes for compensation in activity, but Black has only to develop calmly.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2.strategy: Keeps the d-file blocked, so that ...dxe4 does not force an exchange of queens as it would after Nf3. White chooses a slow, solid set-up: pieces behind the pawn on e4, and the plan of building a kingside attack from there with a later e-pawn advance.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4 a second time, so White must keep the pawn protected rather than push ahead. Black commits to a classical set-up and still has a choice of how to challenge White's centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 Nf6 4.Ngf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and keeps the d2-knight as a second defender of e4. The d3 pawn and the d2-knight already guard the pawn against its two attackers, so White has no hurry in the centre; the set-up is flexible and waits to see how Black arranges the pieces.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 Nf6 4.Ngf3 c5.strategy: The classical counter: the pawn contests d4 and gains queenside space. Black plans to castle and play on the queenside while White goes for the kingside, so it is a race of plans in a closed game.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 Nf6 4.Ngf3 Nc6.strategy: Prepares to trade on e4 and put a pawn on e5, which would shut in a fianchettoed king's bishop. A direct approach: Black builds a broad centre instead of the queenside play that the c-pawn offers.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 Nf6 4.Ngf3 c5 5.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop, the characteristic set-up of this system: the bishop will aim at the centre and the king castles behind a compact pawn shield. Slow and solid, with the advance of the e-pawn as the long-term plan to cramp Black.
Develops with pressure on d4: pawn and knight together fight for the square, so White cannot easily play in the centre with the d-pawn. Black gets a harmonious set-up and prepares to castle.

Develops the king's bishop and clears the way to castling. The bishop is hemmed in behind its own pawn and knight for now, the price of this compact set-up; the game stays closed and strategic, and White's plan is the e-pawn advance.
Gets the king's bishop out and prepares castling. The cost is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in behind the pawn on e6, so Black plays a solid but slightly passive game.

1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 Nf6 4.Ngf3 Nc6 5.B.name: French Defence: Reversed Philidor Formation
1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 Nf6 4.Ngf3 Nc6 5.B.strategy: Develops the bishop to e2 instead of fianchettoing: e4 is held by the d-pawn and the d2-knight, and castling is one move away. A flexible set-up that keeps a compact pawn centre and waits to see whether Black pushes in the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5 3.d5.name: Benoni Defence: French Benoni
1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5 3.d5.strategy: Gains space and attacks e6, though the pawn there is defended twice and nothing is lost. If Black trades on d5, the e-file opens and White's pawn on d5 takes the c6 and e6 squares from Black's pieces; if Black does not, White has a cramping wedge in the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5 3.exf5.name: French Defence: Franco-Hiva Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5 3.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn, the right answer to a move that develops nothing and weakens the king's diagonal. If Black recaptures with the e-pawn, the e-file and the e8–h5 diagonal are open in front of the king, and White simply develops with the easier game.

1.e4 e6 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops, but leaves e4 to its fate: after the capture the pawn on e4 attacks the knight, so White loses time as well as a pawn. A knight outpost on e5 backed by the f-pawn and some activity are thin compensation.

1.e4 e6 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4.name: French Defence: La Bourdonnais Variation, Reuter Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn White left hanging, with a gain of time because the pawn attacks the knight. Black has to finish development safely and keep the extra material; White's only compensation is activity, not structure.

1.e4 e6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d4.strategy: Builds the full pawn centre and transposes into the main French with the knight already on c3. White has more space and a defended e4 pawn, and Black must now find a way to fight that centre.

1.e4 e6 2.Nc3 d5 3.f4.name: French Defence: Pelikan Variation
1.e4 e6 2.Nc3 d5 3.f4.strategy: Prepares e5 and a kingside attack instead of building the d4–e4 centre. The cost is the e1–h4 diagonal, open in front of the king (after a trade on e4, ...Qh4+ comes with check), and no central pressure on Black, who can develop and strike back at ease.

1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nc3.name: French Defence: Two Knights Variation
1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and keeps White's options open: the game can become an ordinary French after d4, or a cramping e5 advance. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so White commits to a piece-based set-up and builds the pawn centre later.

1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e5.strategy: Cramps Black's kingside by denying the g8 knight its natural square, and fixes the centre. The e5 pawn is held only by the knight, so Black will attack its base on d4, and White has to support the chain with pieces and pawns.

1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e5 c5.strategy: The standard counter to a pawn chain: Black attacks its base at once, before White has put a pawn on d4, where only the knight guards the square. The e5 pawn loses its natural support, and White must defend the centre rather than expand.

1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e5 c5 4.b4.name: French Defence: Wing Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e5 c5 4.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to pull Black's c-pawn away so that a pawn centre can be built without pressure on d4. The pawn is real, though, and the queenside is loosened; Black can take it and keep the solid structure.
